name: Arah
title: Israelite patriarch of a family that returned from the Babylonian exile
lifespan: Unknown, probably before the Babylonian exile (before c. 586 B.C.)
summary: Arah is an Israelite patriarch whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile to Judah. His family is listed in the returnee registers in Ezra 2:5 with 775 people and in Nehemiah 7:10 with 652 people – a numerical difference that likely reflects different times of registration or counting criteria. In 1 Chronicles 7:39, the name Arah appears as a descendant of Asher through Ulla, but it is uncertain whether this refers to the same patriarch mentioned in the returnee lists. Arah's family is also known through his descendant Shekanja, who according to Nehemiah 6:18 was the father-in-law of Tobiah, an Ammonite leader. This marital alliance between a prominent Israelite clan and a foreign leader created significant political tensions during Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem and his efforts to establish religious and ethnic boundaries for the Jewish community.

keyEvents.title: Descendants of Arah in Ezra's list of returnees
keyEvents.description: In the list of those who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel, the descendants of Arah are recorded as 775 people.

keyEvents.title: Descendants of Arah in Nehemiah's list of returnees
keyEvents.description: In Nehemiah's register of the returnees, the descendants of Arah are listed as 652 people, a differing count likely due to different recording circumstances.

keyEvents.title: Shekaniah, son of Arah, and the alliance with Tobiah
keyEvents.description: Shekaniah, a descendant of Arah, was the father-in-law of Tobiah, the Ammonite leader. This marital alliance between an Israelite family and a foreign leader created political complications for Nehemiah's reform work in Jerusalem.

keyEvents.title: Arah in the Genealogy of Asher
keyEvents.description: A person named Arah is mentioned as the son of Ulla in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher. It is unclear whether this is the same person as the ancestor listed in the returnee records.

keyEvents.title: Nehemiah Finds the Genealogy of the Returnees
keyEvents.description: Nehemiah found the genealogy of those who had first returned from Babylon, and Arah's descendants were among the registered families.

versions.summary: Arah was an Israelite whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile. He is mentioned in the genealogies in Ezra and Nehemiah as the ancestor of a family that was among those who returned to Judah. His descendants numbered 775 according to Ezra 2:5 and 652 according to Nehemiah 7:10.
versions.title: Israelite Patriarch After the Exile
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Israelite patriarch after the exile' is somewhat imprecise. Arah was likely a patriarch who lived before the exile, while his descendants returned after the exile. The title should reflect this better.; [major] Arah himself was probably a patriarch who lived before the exile, perhaps in the period before or during the exile. His descendants returned in the 'return' period, but Arah himself likely belongs to an earlier era. Nevertheless, since he is primarily known from the return lists, 'return' can be defended as the context in which he appears. Keep it, but this should be noted.; [minor] Arah's lifespan is difficult to determine. If he was a patriarch for families returning around 538 BC, he may have lived earlier than the 500s BC. A more precise indication would be 'Unknown, probably before the 500s BC' or similar.; [major] There is no biblical indication that Arah was a 'leader'. He is only mentioned as a patriarch in genealogies. 'Patriarch' would be a more accurate role.; [minor] Shekanja (Neh 6:18) is mentioned as the 'son of Arah'. It is possible this refers to a more distant descendant rather than a direct son, but the biblical text uses 'son of'. The relationship can be kept, but it should be noted in a footnote.; [major] In Nehemiah 6:18, it is Shekanja son of Arah who is mentioned, and it says that Tobiah was married to Shekanja's daughter (not 'his daughter was married to Tobiah' as if it were Arah's daughter). The description should be clarified: it was Shekanja's daughter who was married to Tobiah.; [minor] The summary is fine, but it lacks the information that Arah is also mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:39 as a descendant of Asher. This is important for a complete profile.; [major] Footnotes are missing. The profile should include footnotes about the difference between the numbers in Ezra and Nehemiah, the possible identification with Arah in 1 Chronicles 7:39, and the meaning of the name.

versions.summary: Arah is an Israelite known as the ancestor of a family that returned from the Babylonian exile to Judah. He is mentioned in the genealogies in Ezra and Nehemiah among the families who returned with Zerubbabel. According to Ezra 2:5, his descendants numbered 775 people, while Nehemiah 7:10 gives the figure as 652. A person named Arah is also mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:39 as a descendant of Asher, but it is uncertain whether this is the same person. Shekaniah, called the son of Arah, is mentioned in Nehemiah 6:18 in connection with a marriage alliance with Tobiah, the Ammonite leader.
versions.title: Israelite Patriarch Mentioned in the Returnee Lists
versions.reason: [major] According to Nehemiah 6:18, it was Johanan son of Shekanja who had taken as wife the daughter of Meshullam son of Berekiah, and through this connection Tobiah had a son-in-law relationship. The text states that Tobiah was the son-in-law of Shekanja son of Arah – meaning it was Tobiah’s wife who was the daughter of Shekanja, not that Shekanja’s daughter was married to Tobiah in the way the description might suggest. The description should be clarified: Shekanja son of Arah was the father-in-law of Tobiah the Ammonite.; [minor] Shekanja is described in Nehemiah 6:18 as 'son of Arah', but it is unclear whether this means a direct son or a more distant descendant. It may be worth noting this uncertainty, though it is acceptable to retain the wording as is.; [minor] The summary states that 'Shekanja, called son of Arah' was mentioned in connection with 'a marriage alliance with the Ammonite leader Tobiah'. It should be clarified that Tobiah was the son-in-law of Shekanja (Shekanja’s daughter was married to Tobiah), not merely a vague 'marriage alliance'.; [minor] The title 'ancestor' is correct, but one might also consider adding 'clan head' or similar, since he is regarded as the founder of one of the families recorded in the lists of returnees.; [minor] The title is clear, but could be made slightly more specific, for example by mentioning that he is the ancestor of one of the families who returned from Babylon.

versions.summary: Arah is known as the patriarch of an Israelite family that returned from the Babylonian exile to Judah. The family is listed in the returnee registers in both Ezra and Nehemiah among those who came back with Zerubbabel. Ezra 2:5 states that his descendants numbered 775 people, while Nehemiah 7:10 gives 652 – a difference likely due to different times of registration or counting criteria. A person named Arah also appears in 1 Chronicles 7:39 as a descendant of Asher through Ulla, but it is uncertain whether this is the same individual. In Nehemiah 6:18, Shekaniah son of Arah is mentioned as the father-in-law of Tobiah, an Ammonite leader. This marital alliance created political tensions in connection with Nehemiah's rebuilding work in Jerusalem.
versions.title: Israelite Patriarch of One of the Families in the Returnee Lists
versions.reason: [major] In Nehemiah 6:18 it states that Shekanja son of Arah was the father-in-law of Tobiah. However, it is important to note that identifying Shekanja as a direct son of the patriarch Arah is uncertain—it could equally mean 'descendant of Arah'. Listing 'Shekanja' as a child of Arah is a simplification, but acceptable given the context. Still, consideration should be given to clarifying this point.; [minor] The fourth key event element ('Arah's lineage among the returning families') largely overlaps with the first ('Arah's descendants in Ezra's return list') and uses many of the same verses. Consider replacing it with a reference to 1 Chronicles 7:39 mentioned in the summary, to provide broader coverage.; [minor] The fifth key event element ('Registration in the genealogical record') overlaps significantly with the second ('Arah's descendants in Nehemiah's return list'). A better approach would be to combine these, or replace the fifth with the reference to Arah in 1 Chronicles 7:39.; [minor] The reference to Arah in 1 Chronicles 7:39 as a descendant of Asher is mentioned in the summary and footnotes but lacks its own key event entry. Including this would strengthen the profile.; [minor] The phrasing 'Unknown, probably before the 5th century BC' is somewhat vague. Since the descendants returned around 538–520 BC, it could be clarified that the patriarch lived in an earlier period, for example, before the Babylonian exile.

footnotes.text: The name Arah (Hebrew: ארח) likely means 'wanderer' or 'traveler,' derived from the Hebrew root א-ר-ח, which means 'to wander' or 'to travel along a road.' There is poetic irony in that a man with this name became the ancestor of a family that indeed wandered—from Babylon back to Judah.

The difference between the numbers 775 (Ezra 2:5) and 652 (Nehemiah 7:10) for Arah's descendants is a well-known phenomenon in the returnee lists. Such discrepancies may be due to different times of registration, copyist errors during textual transmission, or differing criteria for who was included—for example, whether only men or entire families were counted.

In 1 Chronicles 7:39, an Arah is mentioned as the son of Ulla in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher. Scholars debate whether this is the same person as the ancestor in Ezra and Nehemiah. If it is the same person, it may indicate that some of those who returned from Babylon belonged to the tribes of the northern kingdom, not only Judah and Benjamin.

The connection between Shekaniah's family and the Ammonite leader Tobiah (Neh 6:18) illustrates the complex social and political conditions in Persian-controlled Judah after the exile. Marriage alliances across ethnic and religious boundaries were a persistent point of contention, as also highlighted in Ezra 9–10.

The returnee lists in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 are among the most important sources for understanding the rebuilding of the Jewish community after the exile. They organize the returnees by family heads and provide valuable insight into the social structure of the early Second Temple period (ca. 538–515 BCE).

Tobiah is referred to as 'the Ammonite servant' in Nehemiah 2:10, but his marriage alliances with prominent Jewish families—including Arah's lineage—suggest that he held significant social and political influence. Rabbinic tradition has viewed such intermarriages as a threat to the people's religious identity during the rebuilding period.
